name: Brow dyeing blonde / bleaching

lead: Brow bleaching lightens eyebrow hair, often to blonde, for a distinct look. Dyeing can instead darken brows.
No studies of brow bleaching were found in the sources consulted.

paras: Hydrogen peroxide with an alkaline agent oxidizes melanin in the hair, lightening it. Dyes deposit color.
Irritation, allergic reactions (including to phenylenediamine dyes), breakage and discoloration are documented with hair coloring in general. The eye area is sensitive.

lead: Bleaching or dyeing the eyebrows lighter, often blonde, is a style practice used to soften or alter the look of the brow. Hair bleaching works by oxidizing melanin with hydrogen peroxide in an alkaline mixture, with home products typically around 6% peroxide and salon products up to 12%, according to Wikipedia.[1]

Wikipedia notes that hair coloring can cause skin irritation, allergy and hair breakage, and that phenylenediamine-based dyes can cause allergic reactions that may appear hours or a day later.[1] The sources consulted contain no specific regulatory statements about bleaching eyebrows, and no published studies of brow bleaching were found.
infobox: Hydrogen peroxide, alkaline agents; dyes may contain phenylenediamine

paras: Permanent dye can darken brows to match hair color,[2] while bleaching lightens them by removing pigment.[1] Proponents of bleached brows describe the look as a fashion statement or as a way to shift the facial impression.

Reactions to hair coloring include temporary skin irritation, allergy, breakage, skin discoloration and unexpected color. Manufacturers often recommend a patch test, while some European dermatologists have advised against pre-use testing because it can itself sensitize.[1] The eye area is delicate, and the sources consulted give no product-specific data for brow use.
